findings.explanation: The `Savepoint.rollback_to()` method at line 132-134 constructs a SQL command using an f-string with `self.name` interpolated directly: `f"ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT {self.name}"`. The `name` value is set in `__init__` (line 128) from a `name: str` parameter. This `name` originates from two call sites: (1) `PostgresTransaction.savepoint()` which either accepts a caller-supplied `name` argument or generates one automatically as `f"savepoint_{self.get_savepoint_id()}"`, and (2) `PostgresTransaction.rollback_to(savepoint_name: str)` which passes `savepoint_name` directly. In case (1), if an application passes a user-controlled string as the savepoint name, it would be interpolated unescaped into the SQL command. There is no validation or sanitization of the `name` value before interpolation, and no parameterized query mechanism is used (savepoint names cannot be bound as parameters in standard SQL, but a whitelist/identifier-quoting approach would be appropriate). This constitutes a potential SQL injection if user-controlled input reaches the `name` argument.

findings.explanation: The documented security contract for transactions states: 'If an exception is raised within the body of the context manager, then the transaction is automatically rolled back. The exception is still propagated though.' The new nested `__aexit__` logic in both Postgres and SQLite engines violates the second half of this guarantee. When `self._parent` is set (i.e., the block is a nested transaction), `__aexit__` returns `True` when there is NO exception (`return exception is None` evaluates to `True` when `exception is None`). However, when an exception IS raised inside the nested block, `exception is None` is `False`, so the method returns `False` — this part is correct. BUT the outer `__aexit__` (the parent transaction) still has `return exception is None` at its end (line 264 in postgres.py, line 437 in sqlite.py), which suppresses the exception at the outer level too. More critically, the nested exit at line 245-246 (postgres) and 422-423 (sqlite) returns `False` on exception, allowing it to propagate — but it does NOT trigger the outer transaction's rollback path because the parent transaction's `__aexit__` is called independently with the same exception and returns `exception is None`. When the outer context manager's `__aexit__` receives the exception it does call rollback (lines 248-251 / 425-428), so in isolation rollback is triggered. However, the nested `__aexit__` returning `exception is None` (True when no exception) unconditionally suppresses the exception for no-exception cases but silently ignores that the inner block may have executed writes that the user expected to be rolled back independently. The more direct authorization-relevant concern is: the nested exit at line 245-246 returns `True` (suppressing the exception entirely) when there is NO exception, which means an exception thrown deeper inside the nested block that was somehow caught and re-raised at that point would be silently swallowed at the nested level, preventing the outer transaction from knowing a failure occurred in a nested scope. This is an incorrect authorization/integrity control because the policy requires exceptions to always propagate.

findings.suggested_fix: When `self._parent` is set and there is an exception (`exception is not None`), the nested `__aexit__` should NOT suppress the exception. It should always return `False` (or re-raise) so the exception propagates to the outer transaction context manager, which can then perform the rollback as documented. Change `return exception is None` to `return False` (or simply `return None`) so exceptions always propagate out of nested transaction blocks.

.. _Transactions:

Transactions
============

Transactions allow multiple queries to be committed only once successful.

This is useful for things like migrations, where you can't have it fail in an
inbetween state.

.. note::
    In the examples below we use ``MyTable._meta.db`` to access the ``Engine``,
    which is used to create transactions.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Atomic
------

This is useful when you want to programmatically add some queries to the
transaction before running it.

.. code-block:: python

    transaction = Band._meta.db.atomic()
    transaction.add(Manager.create_table())
    transaction.add(Concert.create_table())
    await transaction.run()

    # You're also able to run this synchronously:
    transaction.run_sync()

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Transaction
-----------

This is the preferred way to run transactions - it currently only works with
async.

.. code-block:: python

    async with Band._meta.db.transaction():
        await Manager.create_table()
        await Concert.create_table()

If an exception is raised within the body of the context manager, then the
transaction is automatically rolled back. The exception is still propagated
though.

``transaction_exists``
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

You can check whether your code is currently inside a transaction using the
following:

.. code-block:: python

    >>> Band._meta.db.transaction_exists()
    True

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Transaction types
-----------------

SQLite
~~~~~~

For SQLite you may want to specify the :ref:`transaction type <SQLiteTransactionTypes>`,
as it can have an effect on how well the database handles concurrent requests.

``BaseUser`` is a ``Table`` you can use to store and authenticate your users.

The app comes with some useful commands.

~~~~~~

Creates a new user. It presents an interactive prompt, asking for the username,
password etc.

.. code-block:: bash

    piccolo user create

script), you can pass all of the arguments in as follows:

.. code-block:: bash

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

    piccolo user change_password

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Change a user's permissions. The options are ``--admin``, ``--superuser`` and
``--active``, which change the corresponding attributes on ``BaseUser``.
